In the previous exercise you have learnt how to create a very simple GLM. The model is truly simple and almost not usable for real-life applications, as its results are very similar to one-way analysis.

We need to improve it by adding other variables and using the best data we have available. So we will iterate over many combinations of features and their transformations to improve the model.

`But how do we know model is performing well?`

There are several methods to assess the model performance, but we will focus on a few only. Using these methods you split your data into **training** and **validation** subsets to ensure the model is robust and doesn't overfit the current data, but is prepared to work on future data we have not seen yet.

### Validation Methods

A few methods to split the data:

1.  Out of sample validation (randomly split into two pieces, e.g. 80% vs. 20% of data)
2.  Out of time validation (split into two pieces using some time variable, e.g. years 2012-2016 vs. year 2017)
3.  Cross validation (randomly split into k pieces (folds); k-1 folds together are used for training and the remaining fold for validation, and this is repeated so that every fold is the validation fold once)

![validation methods](/cloud/project/Support/img_D_validation_methods.png)

Once you split your data into training and validation parts, you fit the GLM on the training data only, and then use the validation data to get an idea about the performance on unseen data.

```{r cell_01}
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
# load data, this is the dataset from Lesson 4 where we prepared Claims with Policies into one dataset
dt_pol_w_claims <- readRDS("/cloud/project/Data/dt_pol_w_claims_target.rds")
```

```{r cell_02}
# split the dataset into Modeling and Validation part
set.seed(58742) # to fix randomizer

n_rows <- nrow(dt_pol_w_claims)
train_idx <- sample(n_rows, round(0.80*n_rows)) # 80/20 split between train and valid

train <- dt_pol_w_claims[train_idx, ]
valid <- dt_pol_w_claims[-train_idx, ]

nrow(train)
nrow(valid)
```

### Validation Metric

When you have predictions, you can compare actual values with predictions and assess how the model performs.

Once again there are a couple of **metrics** to choose from, and the choice depends on the type of the model you are trying to create.

A few metrics to evaluate the performance of a regression model:

1.  Root Mean Squared Error $$RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i-\hat{x_i})^2}{N}}$$
2.  Mean Absolute Error
3.  Median Absolute Error
4.  R2 Score

For inspiration, here is a nice summary of the metric functions (created for Python): <http://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html>. See also `Support/Metrics.Rmd`.

All of those metrics can be implemented very easily in R and we will create a simple methodology to do that.

For the future, I would like to mention the packages `caret` and `tidymodels`, which automate some of the actions we need to do manually here.

```{r cell_03}
# definition of the RMSE metric
rmse <- function(actual, prediction){
  se <- (prediction-actual)^2
  mse <- mean(se)
  sqrt(mse)
}

actuals <- c(1.5, 0.5, 2.5, 9.5, 4, 7, 2, 0, 0.1, 12, 3, 2)
predicted <- c(3.7, 1.8, 2.2, 10, 3.6, 6.5, 1.2, -0.6, 1.8, 11.9, 3.1, 2.2)
rmse(actuals, predicted)
```

Let's think for a second about how insurance works. In the early lessons we mentioned that insurance is risk pooling. Many people pay a small amount of money (premium) so that the insurance company is able to pay out the few people that have claims (a high amount of money).

Since we do not expect everybody to have a claim, we neither expect nor desire to predict every observation correctly - a lot of them have and will have zero losses. Rather, we want to make sure that bigger groups / segments of our dataset are predicted correctly.

We will therefore sort our dataset by increasing predictions (risk) from the least risky to the most risky, then divide it into N groups of roughly equal size (weight). We then make sure that the actual and predicted values of losses match in these groups, rather than on every single observation.

Step 1 - sort the data by the prediction, cut it into groups and average the actual and predicted values within each group:

![grouped RMSE step 1](/cloud/project/Support/img_E1_group_the_data.png)

Step 2 - compare the group means. The same idea can be drawn as a chart of actual vs. predicted values per group - a **lift chart**, which we will use in the next exercise. The noise of individual policies is averaged out and the signal becomes visible. The RMSE is then computed over the groups only:

![grouped RMSE step 2](/cloud/project/Support/img_E2_compare_groups.png)

```{r cell_04}
# improved RMSE metric computed on an ordered and grouped data
rmse_group <- function(actual, prediction, weight=NULL, n_groups=5) {
  if(is.null(weight)) {
    weight <- rep(1, length(actual))
  }
  
  if(n_groups>0) {
    # order by increasing prediction
    prediction_order <- order(prediction)
    prediction <- prediction[prediction_order]
    actual <- actual[prediction_order]
    weight <- weight[prediction_order]
    
    # split into 'n_groups'
    prediction_group <- cut(seq_along(prediction), n_groups, labels=FALSE)
    prediction_split <- split(prediction, prediction_group)
    actual_split <- split(actual, prediction_group)
    weight_split <- split(weight, prediction_group)
    
    # compute actual and prediction by group
    prediction <- purrr::map2_dbl(prediction_split, weight_split, weighted.mean)
    actual <- purrr::map2_dbl(actual_split, weight_split, weighted.mean)
  }
  
  se <- (prediction-actual)^2
  mse <- mean(se)
  sqrt(mse)
}

actuals <- c(1.5, 0.5, 2.5, 9.5, 4, 7, 2, 0, 0.1, 12, 3, 2)
predicted <- c(3.7, 1.8, 2.2, 10, 3.6, 6.5, 1.2, -0.6, 1.8, 11.9, 3.1, 2.2)
weight <- c(3L, 1L, 3L, 4L, 2L, 5L, 1L, 4L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L)

rmse(actuals, predicted)
rmse_group(actuals, predicted, n_groups=0)  # no grouping - same as rmse()
rmse_group(actuals, predicted, n_groups=3)  # 12 observations in 3 groups of 4
rmse_group(actuals, predicted, weight, n_groups=5)  # weighted group means
```

Averaging within groups cancels out much of the noise of individual observations: with 3 groups the RMSE drops from about 0.97 to 0.39. (With the weights and 5 groups the groups are different, so the value, about 0.63, is not directly comparable.) The same function is stored in `Support/rmse_group.R`, so in the next exercise we will just load it with `source()`.
